identification.bodyShape: Relatively small, stout-bodied rockfish with a high dorsal fin carrying particularly long spines and deeply notched forward dorsal fin membranes (CDFW, WDFW).
identificationTraits: Long, prominent dorsal spines with membranes notched more deeply than the similar copper rockfish (CDFW, ADFG).
Pale yellow or orange markings between the eyes and pectoral fins, plus speckling on the dorsal surface (CDFW).

Dorsal fin spines are white or light yellow, sometimes with dark brown or black saddle markings; some individuals show brown or orange freckling on the head, though this is less common in Puget Sound fish (WDFW).
Distinguished from brown rockfish by the lack of a gill-cover spot, and from copper rockfish by the lack of lateral-line bands and eye radiations (WDFW).
identification.coloration: Orange-brown to black body, described by ADFG as brown mottled with orange and yellow, with the pale head/pectoral markings and dorsal speckling noted above (CDFW, ADFG, WDFW).
identification.adultAppearance: A stout, dark orange-brown to black rockfish with a tall, long-spined, deeply notched dorsal fin and pale head and dorsal markings.

similarSpecies.name: Copper rockfish (Sebastes caurinus)
similarSpecies.distinction: Copper rockfish shares some dorsal-fin notching but quillback's is more pronounced; copper rockfish also shows lateral-line bands and eye radiations that quillback lacks (CDFW, WDFW). Because bag limits in this fishery are species-specific, this is the most consequential confusion pair for anglers.

similarSpecies.name: Brown rockfish (Sebastes auriculatus)
similarSpecies.distinction: Brown rockfish carries a dark spot on the gill cover that quillback lacks (WDFW).

identification.averageAdultLength: California specimens run smaller than the northern part of the range — at age 12, California quillback average about 7.1 in (CDFW). Males mature at about 8.7 in (age 4) and females at about 10.2 in (age 6) in California (CDFW); COSEWIC gives 50% maturity in British Columbia at roughly age 11.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Legal minimum sizes and sub-bag limits vary sharply by state and are unusually likely to have changed recently for this species — see targetContext before advising an angler.
identification.typicalWeight: WDFW gives a maximum of about 3.3 kg (7.2 lb) at maximum length; typical landed fish are considerably smaller.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: About 24 in maximum length in California (CDFW); WDFW gives a maximum length of 63.6 cm (25 in).
identification.longevity: California fish have been aged to 15 years; Canadian populations reach at least 76-95 years, with females outliving males (about 80 years maximum for males) (CDFW, COSEWIC, WDFW).

social.byLifeStage: Juveniles occupy shallower nearshore rocky habitat of varying complexity; adults move into deeper water and become largely solitary reef-dwellers, perched on rocks or sheltering in crevices and holes (CDFW).
social.note: COSEWIC and CDFW both describe a limited home range (on the order of 10 m^2 in one cited study) with strong site fidelity — displaced fish have been documented returning to their home reef.

feedingStrategy.note: Adults take crustaceans (especially shrimp), small fish, clams, marine worms, and fish eggs; larvae and juveniles feed on planktonic organisms and eggs (CDFW, COSEWIC).

behavior.territoriality: Not documented as actively territorial toward other fish; the dominant pattern reported is a small, defended-by-site-fidelity home range on a single reef (COSEWIC).

dielTendency.note: Diel feeding pattern is not documented in the sources reviewed for this record; see gaps.

behavior.depthMovement: Juveniles settle in shallower nearshore rocky habitat than adults, which range from the surface to about 900 ft, with most commercial catch concentrated at 46-470 ft (CDFW, COSEWIC).
behavior.coverUse: Hard, complex substrate with vertical relief — broken rock, reefs, ridges and crevices — is specifically identified as a habitat requirement, not just a preference (COSEWIC).
behavior.spawningBehavior: Internal fertilization with mating in December; females can store sperm for weeks before fertilization, and parturition (live birth) occurs April-May in British Columbia (COSEWIC) or April-July in California (CDFW). This is conservation context only — holding water around a parturition-stage aggregation is excluded from target guidance.

diet.primaryNote: Adults feed on a variety of prey — CDFW specifically names crustaceans (especially shrimp), small fish, clams, marine worms, and fish eggs; COSEWIC broadly describes adult diet as fishes plus benthic and pelagic invertebrates, especially shrimp. Larvae and juveniles take planktonic organisms and eggs (CDFW). Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.juvenile: Planktonic organisms and eggs, shifting toward benthic prey as fish settle onto nearshore rocky habitat (CDFW).
lifeStageDiet.adult: Crustaceans (especially shrimp), small fish, clams, marine worms, and fish eggs (CDFW, COSEWIC).

diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity is not proof that a particular prey event is occurring at a given time. Observed current forage still comes from a user observation or Hatch Match.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Quillback rockfish are sedentary, crevice-holding reef residents on hard, high-relief substrate. The clearest seasonal signal is a winter mating-to-spring parturition window, which is conservation context only. Regulatory status for this species has changed repeatedly in the past three years — verify current sub-bag limits and any depth closure before fishing (see targetContext).

entries.habitatClass: Solitary positions in rock crevices and holes on hard, high-relief reef structure.
entries.conservationNote: Mating occurs in December, with females able to store sperm for weeks before fertilization (COSEWIC). This is conservation context, not a location cue.
entries.presentationImplication: Drop-presentation and bottom-contact worked into crevice structure remain the reviewed nearshore families; check current-year closures and sub-bag limits first.
invalidators: assuming a specific reef holds a mating aggregation
assuming the same season/bag rules apply as last year given recent regulatory changes

entries.habitatClass: Hard, high-relief reef structure as parturition occurs.
entries.conservationNote: Parturition (live birth) runs April-May in British Columbia and April-July in California. This is conservation context only (COSEWIC, CDFW).
entries.presentationImplication: Drop-presentation and bottom-contact nearshore; vertical-jig and deep-drop offshore.
invalidators: treating a parturition-stage aggregation as a location to target
